splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on when actuarial assumptions must be finalized for calculating withdrawal liability under ERISA's multiemployer pension provisions. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be fixed by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about the limits of judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, allowing courts to find violations and impose consequences even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release terms run continuously regardless of absconding, and courts lack authority to apply a common-law tolling doctrine to extend punishment beyond the statutory term.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar from raising any claim they previously presented in successive collateral attacks under Section 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement; if not, they need only satisfy 2255(h)'s requirements of showing newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners filing § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy the requirements of § 2255(h).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome determines whether such disputes can be adjudicated before elections or must be funneled into post-election litigation, with implications for challenges to mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules before an election based on competitive injury from allegedly unlawful voting procedures.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to state voting procedures because they cannot demonstrate concrete, particularized injury.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Jacobson v. Florida Secretary of State

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous provisions that carry criminal or quasi-criminal consequences.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts should apply the rule of lenity or defer to agency/Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous Sentencing Guidelines or criminal provisions. This split has deepened after Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo overruled Chevron deference, casting further doubt on whether deference can override lenity in criminal contexts.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous provisions with criminal consequences, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes precedence over the rule of lenity, allowing deference to an anti-defendant reading of ambiguous Guidelines enhancements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), or whether possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. This governs whether district courts must impose sentences without regard to statutory minimums and affects criminal sentencing uniformity nationwide.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as disjunctive or distributive in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, based on Application Note 1's commentary, or whether the guideline text unambiguously excludes them.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds conspiracy, aiding and abetting, and attempt to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid authoritative interpretation of the guideline or impermissibly expands its text. This split affects career-offender designations for defendants with prior inchoate drug offense convictions.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation under Stinson v. United States and Kisor v. Wilkie, and that 'controlled substance offense' includes conspiracy and other inchoate offenses.

positions.label: Guideline text excludes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) is unambiguous and does not include inchoate offenses, and that Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline's scope beyond its plain text.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply divided on whether non-retroactive changes in law — particularly the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory consecutive 'stacked' sentences for § 924(c) gun offenses — can be considered as a factor supporting compassionate release. Some circuits categorically prohibit consideration of such changes while others allow them as one factor among many.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as one factor among others when evaluating whether extraordinary and compelling reasons warrant compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state controls a substance not listed on federal schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally controlled, or whether any state-controlled substance suffices. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements based on prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State schedules suffice — no federal-law limitation
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under § 4B1.2(b) includes state drug offenses regardless of whether the substance is controlled under federal law, finding no textual basis to graft a federal limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the underlying substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's property belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This question significantly affects debtor protections and creditor recoveries in converted bankruptcy cases.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), coupled with the broad definition of 'property of the estate' in § 541(a), means post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure, purpose, and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor in a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the terms (but not necessarily the fact or duration) of imprisonment must proceed via habeas corpus or may use other statutory vehicles such as Bivens actions.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP administrative decisions like denials of transfer to prerelease custody. This affects how prisoners can challenge FSA time credit applications and other BOP decisions.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for duration-related claims
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner challenges BOP decisions affecting the fact or duration of confinement (including prerelease custody decisions), habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 is the exclusive federal remedy.

positions.label: Conditions claims may proceed outside habeas
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement or BOP administrative decisions that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment may proceed through civil rights actions rather than habeas.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to an order denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment, given that the motion is filed in a criminal case but seeks a civil remedy.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is governed by the 30-day civil appeal deadline or the 14-day criminal appeal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because a Hyde Amendment motion is filed in and arises from a criminal case, the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly consider punishment when imposing a sentence upon revocation of supervised release, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to sanctions addressing the breach of trust and promoting reentry.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether punishment is a permissible purpose of revocation sentences for supervised release violations. The Sixth Circuit allows express punishment at revocation, while other circuits restrict revocation sentences to addressing the breach of trust and promoting rehabilitation and reentry.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, not merely sanction the breach of trust.

positions.label: Revocation sentences limited to breach of trust / reentry
positions.summary: Holds that revocation of supervised release is not primarily about punishment but about addressing the breach of trust and promoting the defendant's successful reentry into the community.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting or enforcing laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any motor carrier,' extends to common-law negligence claims against freight brokers. This affects the liability framework for the freight brokerage industry nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted because they are general common-law duties of care rather than laws specifically 'related to' broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Commission exceeded its statutory authority by promulgating U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6), which allows non-retroactive changes in law to support compassionate release, when Congress did not make those changes retroactive.
splits.description: Circuits are splitting on whether the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment allowing prisoners serving unusually long sentences due to non-retroactive legal changes to seek compassionate release exceeds the Commission's delegated authority. The Seventh Circuit held the amendment exceeds the Commission's power, while other circuits have or may reach different conclusions.

positions.label: Commission exceeded its authority
positions.summary: Holds that § 1B1.13(b)(6) exceeds the Sentencing Commission's statutory authority because allowing non-retroactive changes in law to support compassionate release is inconsistent with Congress's decision not to make those changes retroactive.

positions.label: Commission acted within its authority
positions.summary: Holds that § 1B1.13(b)(6) is a valid exercise of the Commission's delegated authority to define 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Post-Bruen, circuits have split on whether the federal ban on firearm possession by unlawful drug users passes constitutional muster under the Second Amendment's historical-tradition test. Some circuits have upheld § 922(g)(3) as consistent with historical traditions of disarming dangerous persons, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of disarming those who pose a danger to themselves or others, and survives Second Amendment scrutiny even as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government cannot identify a sufficient historical tradition of disarming persons solely for drug use.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Second Circuit's approach to legal standards governing discrimination claims in hospitality and business contexts, indicating the Court found the approach sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant review and suggesting a circuit split on the applicable standards.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied its own framework for evaluating discrimination claims in hospitality establishments, which the Supreme Court found warranted review.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied different or conflicting standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business establishments, creating the split that prompted certiorari.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether legal errors or constitutional claims that could have been raised in a § 2255 habeas petition may also serve as the basis for compassionate release. Some circuits permit courts to consider such claims as one factor, while others hold that compassionate release cannot be used as a substitute for habeas review.

positions.label: May consider conviction-related errors
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: May not use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A) may not be used as a vehicle to challenge the validity of a conviction or sentence, as those claims must be raised through § 2255 habeas proceedings.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the Section 1 exemption for transportation workers, particularly whether last-mile delivery workers who distribute goods to retail stores are 'engaged in . . . interstate commerce.' This affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a wide range of distribution workers.

positions.label: Broad exemption — last-mile delivery workers qualify
positions.summary: Holds that workers who are part of a continuous interstate transportation chain, including those making last-mile deliveries of goods that have moved in interstate commerce, qualify as transportation workers exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow exemption — last-mile distributors do not qualify
positions.summary: Holds that distribution workers delivering goods locally to retail stores are not 'transportation workers engaged in . . . interstate commerce' under Section 1 because they are not themselves moving goods across state lines.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claims are based on labeling that the EPA approved. This affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticides nationwide.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would require labeling different from or in addition to what the EPA has approved.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because they impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements, consistent with the Supreme Court's Bates v. Dow Agrosciences framework.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
